messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Linh Tran is a 52-year-old Vietnamese-American woman who works as a librarian at a mid-sized public library in the Pacific Northwest. She is married and has lived in the United States for over two decades. She presented for psychological assessment with a PCL-5 score of 61, describing a presentation that has progressively worsened over the fourteen months since she survived a catastrophic flash flood that tore through a rural valley town where she had been visiting extended family. The flood struck without warning in the early hours of the morning. Linh woke in complete darkness to a silence that felt wrong — the kind of absolute stillness that precedes disaster — and within seconds that silence was obliterated by the sound of water crashing through the walls. She spent hours clinging to debris in the dark, surrounded by the voices and then the absence of voices of people she knew. Several of her relatives perished. By the time she was pulled to safety, dawn had barely broken, and the world she had known the night before was gone.

In the months that followed, Linh found that the memory did not stay in the past. It existed instead as something that could be summoned without her consent by almost anything — a sudden hush falling over the library stacks, the faces of her surviving relatives when they visited, the moment each evening when the light faded from the windows. These triggers did not merely remind her of the flood; they returned her to it. Something in her surroundings could instantly reconstitute the full sensory weight of that night, and when the memory forced its way back in, what accompanied it was not fear alone but an overwhelming grief — for the family members lost, for the person she had been before, for the ordinary life that had been swept away. That grief, in turn, made the memory itself feel even more dangerous to approach, and so the memory began to function as a trigger in its own right, each recollection seeding the conditions for the next intrusion.

At work, the library's particular quiet — the professional silence she had once found restorative — became a source of dread. Linh began choosing her seat at the reference desk based on which position gave her the clearest sightlines to the exits. She scanned the reading room compulsively, tracking the movements of patrons, noting who entered and who left. Any colleague connected to the period of the disaster — a coworker who had sent condolences, a regular patron who had asked about the flood — could activate the same hyperalert state that the silence itself produced. This constant threat monitoring kept her nervous system primed, and in that primed state, ordinary sensory details became potential alarms, so that the very act of scanning for danger increased the number of things that felt dangerous, and the triggers multiplied.

To manage this, Linh developed a set of strategies that offered momentary relief but gradually narrowed her world. She began deliberately dissociating — consciously trying to blank out, to feel herself leave her body — when the threat-monitoring became unbearable. She stopped exercising, because the elevated heart rate and physical exertion felt too close to the bodily terror of the flood. She avoided any circumstance that carried the texture of that night: darkness, enclosed spaces, situations where she could not see clearly around her. These strategies did provide short-term relief, but they also preserved the conditions for the next crisis. When she dissociated or avoided, she never completed the processing of the memory, so it remained raw and unintegrated, ready to erupt again. The avoidance of darkness meant that nighttime became its own ritual of dread — she slept with lights on, woke frequently, and each time she surfaced into the dark room, the memory was waiting. The dissociation, rather than containing the trauma, seemed to keep it just beneath the surface, so that the triggers she had not faced remained fully potent.

Linh's husband has noticed that she is no longer the person he married — quieter in a different way now, absent even when present. It was he who finally persuaded her to seek help. What Linh fears most is that this is permanent, that the flood did not just take her relatives but took something essential in her. What she hopes, tentatively, is that someone might show her how to be in a quiet room again without drowning.
